ox: Correct. Acidity depends on how stable the conjugate base is. Acetate's negative charge is spread (delocalized) over two oxygens by resonance; ethoxide has its charge stuck on one oxygen. The more stable base means the stronger acid.
Incorrect. A STRONGER O–H bond would make acetic acid harder to ionize, not easier. Bond strength is not the main factor here.
Incorrect. The number of hydrogens does not matter. Only the one acidic hydrogen leaves, and what matters is the stability of what is left behind.
Incorrect. Ethoxide has no resonance stabilization: the methyl group has no π system to share charge with. Resonance is exactly what ethoxide LACKS.

concept.t: Why carboxylic acids are stronger acids than alcohols
p: A stronger acid is one whose conjugate base is more stable. Resonance is one of the four stability factors (Atom, Resonance, Induction, Orbital). Acetate delocalizes its charge across two oxygens; ethoxide cannot. Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is about 10¹¹ times more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16).

x5B_027.trap: Picking bond strength: a stronger O–H bond would make the acid weaker, not stronger.
mem: Stronger acid = more stable conjugate base.
ARIO order of stability factors: Atom, Resonance, Induction, Orbital.
pKa guide: carboxylic acid ≈ 4–5, phenol ≈ 10, alcohol ≈ 16.
x5B_027.sc: Draw the conjugate base. If you can draw a second resonance structure, that acid is stronger.
x5B_027.mn: ARIO: A = Atom (size/electronegativity), R = Resonance, I = Induction, O = Orbital (s-character).
x5B_027.plain: A spread-out charge is a happy charge. Acetate shares its negative charge between two oxygens like two friends carrying one heavy bag; ethoxide carries it alone.

ox: Wrong. Two mistakes. Dispersion is placed first, but for comparable small molecules it is the weakest. Hydrogen bonds are also placed above ion-dipole, but a full charge pulling on a polar molecule is stronger. (Ion-dipole above dipole-dipole is actually right.)
Wrong. Dipole-dipole is weaker than ion-dipole and hydrogen bonds, and hydrogen bonds are not the weakest. This order is scrambled.
Correct. Full charges give the strongest pull (ion-dipole), then hydrogen bonds, then permanent dipoles (dipole-dipole), then London dispersion, which comes from short-lived induced dipoles.
Wrong. It puts hydrogen bonds above ion-dipole and dispersion above dipole-dipole. Both pairs are in the wrong order.

p: Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate molecules. The more charge involved, the stronger the pull. An ion has a full charge, so ion-dipole (an ion near a polar molecule) is strongest.

A hydrogen bond is a special strong dipole-dipole between H on N, O or F and a lone pair. Ordinary dipole-dipole is next. London dispersion (temporary dipoles in any molecule) is weakest for small molecules.

mem: Order: ion-dipole > H-bond > dipole-dipole > London.
H-bond needs H on N, O or F.
London grows with molecule size and electron count.
d_5B_14.trap: Students forget that ion-dipole outranks hydrogen bonds, because full charges pull harder than partial charges.
d_5B_14.plain: Think of magnets. A big fridge magnet is an ion pulling on a polar molecule. A medium magnet is a hydrogen bond. A small craft magnet is a regular dipole-dipole pull. A weak sticker is London dispersion.

ox: Wrong. Base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, which are non-covalent. Covalent bonds hold the backbone together.
Correct. G-C has three hydrogen bonds and A-T has two, and G-C stacks more strongly. More energy (higher temperature) is needed to pull the strands apart.
Wrong. Phosphates are in the sugar-phosphate backbone, not in the pairing. Each nucleotide has one, so the count does not differ by base.
Wrong. Both G and A are purines (two rings). The pyrimidines are C, T and U. This also would not explain melting.

p: Melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which half of the double-stranded DNA has separated into single strands. Strands come apart when hydrogen bonds between bases break.
Guanine pairs with cytosine using three hydrogen bonds. Adenine pairs with thymine using two. More hydrogen bonds means more heat needed, so more G-C means a higher Tm.

mem: G-C: 3 H-bonds. A-T: 2 H-bonds.
More G-C content means higher Tm.
Purines: A, G. Pyrimidines: C, T, U.
d_5B_17.mn: Pure As Gold: Purines are Adenine and Guanine. CUT the Pie: Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine are pyrimidines.
d_5B_17.trap: Mixing up the hydrogen bond counts, or saying the bases are joined covalently.
d_5B_17.plain: Two sheets held together by three pieces of tape are harder to pull apart than two held by two pieces.

ox: Correct. For water, the solid-liquid line slopes backward (negative slope). Raising pressure at a temperature just below 0 C moves you across the line into the liquid region, so ice melts.
Wrong. Where the triple point sits does not explain pressure melting. The slope of the solid-liquid line does.
Wrong. The critical point is about liquid and gas becoming one fluid. It has nothing to do with ice melting.
Wrong. Sublimation (solid to gas) curves slope upward, and this question is about solid to liquid.

p: A phase diagram plots pressure (up) against temperature (across) and shows which phase (solid, liquid, gas) is stable. The lines are where two phases coexist.

For most substances the solid-liquid line leans right. For water it leans left, because ice is less dense than liquid water. Pressure favors the denser phase, which is liquid, so squeezing ice makes it melt.

mem: Water's solid-liquid line has a negative slope.
Ice is less dense than liquid water.
Pressure favors the denser phase.
d_5B_20.trap: Assuming the solid-liquid line always slopes forward as in most substances like CO₂.
d_5B_20.plain: Ice takes up more room than water. Squeeze it and it prefers to turn into water, which is more compact.

ox: Correct. Water forms extensive hydrogen bonds (H on O), so it needs the most energy to boil. It has the highest boiling point.
Wrong. Sulfur is not electronegative enough for strong hydrogen bonds. H₂S is a gas at room temperature despite being larger than H₂O.
Wrong. Methane is nonpolar with only weak London forces, so it boils at a very low temperature.
Wrong. Neon is a single atom with only very weak London forces. It boils extremely low.

p: Boiling means molecules escape the liquid. Stronger attractions between molecules mean a higher boiling point.
Water has hydrogen bonds (H bonded to O, N or F, attracted to a lone pair on a neighbor). H₂S, CH₄ and Ne have only weaker dipole or London forces.

mem: Hydrogen bonding raises boiling point.
H-bond needs H on N, O or F.
Nonpolar small molecules boil lowest.
q72.mn: FON: Fluorine, Oxygen, Nitrogen are the atoms that make H-bonds.
q72.trap: Picking the heaviest molecule. Here hydrogen bonding beats size.
q72.plain: Water molecules hold hands tightly, so it takes a lot of heat to pull them apart into steam.

ox: Wrong. Trigonal planar has three groups and no lone pair. This ignores the lone pair on nitrogen.
Wrong. Tetrahedral is the electron geometry (four electron domains), not the molecular shape. The shape names only the atoms.
Correct. N has four electron domains: three N-H bonds and one lone pair. The lone pair is not counted in the shape, so the shape is trigonal pyramidal.
Wrong. Bent is for two bonds and two lone pairs, like H₂O.

p: VSEPR means electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) spread as far apart as possible. Electron geometry counts all groups. Molecular geometry names only the shape the atoms make.
NH₃ has 4 groups (3 bonds, 1 lone pair), so electron geometry is tetrahedral. Hide the lone pair and the atoms form a pyramid.

mem: 4 groups, 0 lone pairs: tetrahedral (CH₄).
4 groups, 1 lone pair: trigonal pyramidal (NH₃).
4 groups, 2 lone pairs: bent (H₂O).
q73.trap: Giving the electron geometry (tetrahedral) when asked for molecular geometry.
q73.plain: A camera tripod with three legs and a hidden fourth stick pointing up: you only see the three legs.

ox: Correct. Each carbon in HC≡CH has two electron domains (one single bond to H, one triple bond to C), so it is sp hybridized and linear at 180°.
Wrong. sp² is for three domains, like carbons in ethene (C=C). Ethyne has only two domains per carbon.
Wrong. sp³ is for four domains, like ethane. A triple bond uses fewer domains.
Wrong. sp³d needs an expanded octet, and carbon (period 2) cannot do that.

p: Hybridization is mixing atomic orbitals to make new ones for bonding. Count the electron domains (each atom bonded, each lone pair; a double or triple bond counts as one) around the atom.
Two domains means sp, three means sp², four means sp³. A triple bond counts once, so each carbon in ethyne has two domains: sp.

mem: 2 domains: sp, linear, 180°.
3 domains: sp², trigonal planar, 120°.
4 domains: sp³, tetrahedral, 109.5°.
Triple bond = 1 sigma + 2 pi.
q74.trap: Counting each bond of the triple bond as a separate domain.
q74.plain: Two people holding both your hands from opposite sides: you stand in a straight line.

ox: Correct. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. They rotate plane-polarized light by equal amounts in opposite directions (one +, one -).
Wrong. Enantiomers have identical boiling points. Boiling point differences belong to diastereomers or constitutional isomers.
Wrong. In an achiral solvent like water, their solubility is identical. Only a chiral environment tells them apart.
Wrong. They are isomers, so they share the same molecular formula and the same connectivity.

p: A chiral molecule has a mirror image that cannot be laid on top of it. The two mirror images are enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images).

They share all physical properties (melting point, boiling point, density) in a non-chiral setting. The key difference is the direction they rotate plane-polarized light, and how they react with other chiral molecules.

mem: Enantiomers: same physical properties, opposite optical rotation.
Equal and opposite rotation.
Different only with chiral reagents or enzymes.
q75.trap: Thinking enantiomers differ in boiling point or solubility. Diastereomers do, enantiomers do not.
q75.plain: Your left and right hands: same shape and size, but a left glove will not fit the right hand.

ox: Correct. Two stereocenters with an internal mirror plane make a meso compound. Its two halves cancel each other's rotation, so it is achiral and optically inactive.
Wrong. A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of two enantiomers, which is a mixture, not a single molecule.
Wrong. A mirror plane inside the molecule makes it superimposable on its mirror image, so it is achiral and not optically active.
Wrong. Diastereomers describe a relationship between two different molecules. One molecule alone cannot be a pair.

p: A stereocenter is a carbon with four different groups. A molecule with stereocenters is usually chiral, but not always.

If a mirror plane runs inside the molecule, one half is the mirror image of the other half. Their optical rotations cancel. This is a meso compound: achiral and optically inactive despite having stereocenters.

mem: Meso: stereocenters plus internal mirror plane.
Meso is achiral and optically inactive.
Racemic = 50:50 enantiomer mix.
q76.trap: Assuming any molecule with stereocenters is chiral.
q76.plain: A butterfly folded down the middle: the left wing mirrors the right, so the whole thing is symmetric.

ox: Wrong. Complete transfer describes an ionic bond. In a coordinate bond the pair is still shared between N and B.
Correct. In H₃N-BF₃ the nitrogen lone pair supplies both electrons to boron, which has an empty p orbital. N is the Lewis base (electron donor) and B is the Lewis acid (electron acceptor).
Wrong. One electron from each atom is the ordinary covalent bond. In a coordinate bond both electrons come from one atom.
Wrong. The shared pair sits between N and B. The fluorines are on boron and do not donate it.

p: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Usually each atom gives one electron. In a coordinate (dative) bond, one atom gives both electrons.
A Lewis base has a lone pair to give. A Lewis acid has an empty orbital to accept it. Boron in BF₃ has only 6 electrons, so it accepts the lone pair from NH₃.

mem: Coordinate bond: both electrons from one atom.
Lewis base donates a pair, Lewis acid accepts.
Once formed, it acts like any covalent bond.
x5B_004.trap: Thinking the bond is different in kind after forming. It is only different in where the electrons came from.
x5B_004.plain: Two friends share a sandwich. Usually each brings half. In a coordinate bond, one friend brought the whole sandwich and the other brought the empty plate.

ox: Wrong. Forming a bond releases energy, so potential energy falls. It does not rise to the bond and stay flat.
Wrong. Even without gaining or losing electrons, attraction of each electron to both nuclei lowers the energy as the atoms approach.
Wrong. Energy does not keep falling. At very short distances, the two positive nuclei repel strongly and energy shoots up.

Correct. Energy drops as the atoms approach and reaches a minimum at the bond length (the stable distance). Closer than that, nuclear repulsion makes it rise sharply. The depth of the well is the bond energy.

p: Potential energy is stored energy from position. Far apart, two H atoms do not interact, so energy is about zero. As they approach, electrons are attracted to both nuclei and energy goes down.
At the bond length the pull and push balance, giving the lowest energy. Closer than that, the positive nuclei repel each other and energy rises steeply.

mem: Bond length = minimum of the energy curve.
Depth of the well = bond energy.
Too close: nuclear repulsion dominates.
x5B_005.trap: Picking 'continuously decreases'. Repulsion at short range makes the curve turn back up.
x5B_005.plain: Two magnets pulled together settle in a sweet spot. Push them any closer and something shoves back.

ox: Wrong. Phosphorus is in period 3, so it can hold ten electrons. PCl₅ exists.
Wrong. Sulfur is in period 3 and SF₄ exists with an expanded octet (ten electrons).
Correct. Nitrogen is in period 2, with only 2s and 2p orbitals, so it cannot hold more than eight electrons. Five bonds would need ten, so NCl₅ does not exist.
Wrong. Xenon is in period 5, so it expands its octet. XeF₂ has two bonds and three lone pairs, ten electrons in all.

p: The octet rule says atoms like eight valence electrons (outer-shell electrons). Period 2 atoms (C, N, O, F) cannot hold more than eight, since they only have 2s and 2p orbitals.
Atoms in period 3 or lower (P, S, Cl, Xe) can hold more than eight. This is why PCl₅ and SF₆ exist but NCl₅ does not.

mem: Period 2 atoms never exceed eight electrons.
Period 3 and below can expand.
NCl₅ does not exist; PCl₅ does.
x5B_008.trap: Assuming that because N and P are in the same group, they can bond the same way.
x5B_008.plain: A small cup holds only so much juice. A bigger cup (a larger atom) holds more.

ox: Wrong. This is the sign-flipped answer (formed minus broken). Bonds broken cost energy, so the formula is broken minus formed.
Wrong. This counts only one H-Cl bond forming. Two H-Cl bonds form, so 680 - 430 = 250 is wrong.
Wrong. This counts only the energy released (2 x 430 = 860) and ignores the energy needed to break H-H and Cl-Cl.
Correct. ΔH = energy to break bonds minus energy released forming bonds = (440 + 240) - 2(430) = 680 - 860 = -180 kJ. Negative means exothermic.

p: Bond energy is the energy needed to break a bond. Breaking bonds takes energy in. Forming bonds releases energy out.
ΔH (the heat change of the reaction) is energy in minus energy out. If more is released than is put in, ΔH is negative (exothermic).

mem: ΔH = broken - formed.
Negative ΔH = exothermic.
Count every bond, including coefficients.

fm.f: ΔH = (sum of bond energies broken) - (sum of bond energies formed), where ΔH = heat change of the reaction in kJ
fm.v: Broken: H-H = 440, Cl-Cl = 240. Formed: 2 H-Cl = 2 x 430
fm.why: Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it.
fm.nc: Add the broken ones, double 430 to get 860, then subtract.

x5B_010.trap: Subtracting in the wrong order (formed minus broken) or forgetting to double the H-Cl bond count.
x5B_010.plain: Spending money to take toys apart and getting paid for building new ones. If you earn more than you spend, you end up ahead.

ox: Wrong. This form can be written, but it puts the negative charge on N, which is less electronegative than O. It is a lesser contributor.
Wrong. +1 on O and -2 on N create large charges that are far apart. Such separation makes it a minor contributor.
Wrong. With no formal charges the total would be 0, but the ion is -1. The charge must appear somewhere.
Correct. O-C≡N⁻ is written with O⁻ and has the smallest formal charges. The -1 sits on oxygen, the most electronegative atom, which stabilizes it best.

p: Resonance structures are different ways of drawing the same molecule with the same atoms in place. The real molecule is a mix, but some drawings are more important than others.
Pick the one where every atom has an octet, formal charges (the charge an atom would have if electrons were shared equally) are small, and any negative charge sits on the most electronegative atom.

mem: Rank by octets, then smallest formal charges, then charge on most electronegative atom.
Overall charges must add to the ion charge.
Avoid large charges next to each other.
x5B_014.trap: Choosing the structure with the negative on nitrogen, forgetting that oxygen is more electronegative.
x5B_014.plain: If someone must carry a heavy backpack, give it to the strongest person, not the weakest.

ox: Wrong. The all-single-bond structure already gives sulfur an octet (4 bonds = 8 electrons). The double bonds expand it past eight.
Correct. With four single bonds, sulfur has formal charge +2. Making two S=O bonds brings S to 0 and reduces charge separation, which is the textbook reason for drawing them.
Wrong. Experiment shows all four S-O bonds are equal in length. The double-bond drawing is just one resonance form.
Wrong. The total number of valence electrons is fixed at 32 (6 + 4x6 + 2) no matter how it is drawn.

p: Formal charge is valence electrons minus (lone-pair electrons + number of bonds). For S with four single bonds: 6 - (0 + 4) = +2. Each singly bonded O is -1.
Because sulfur is in period 3, it can hold more than eight electrons. Turning two bonds into S=O gives S: 6 - (0 + 6) = 0 and lowers the charges, so many texts draw it that way.

mem: Formal charge = valence - (lone-pair electrons + bonds).
Aim for formal charges near zero.
Total valence electrons in SO₄²⁻ = 32.

fm.f: Formal charge = V - (L + B), where V = valence electrons of the atom, L = nonbonding electrons, B = number of bonds
fm.v: Sulfur: V = 6, L = 0. Four single bonds: B = 4. Two double and two single: B = 6
fm.s: Four single bonds: 6 - (0 + 4) = +2. With two S=O: 6 - (0 + 6) = 0
fm.why: The formal charge shows which drawing has less charge separation.

x5B_019.trap: Thinking the double bonds are needed to complete an octet. They actually reduce formal charge.
x5B_019.plain: Instead of leaving one kid holding two heavy bags while others hold none, spread the load more evenly.

ox: Wrong. Giving all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom is the oxidation-state rule. Mixing up the two bookkeeping systems is the trap.
Correct. For formal charge, every bond is treated as perfectly shared. Each atom gets half of each bonding pair, no matter how electronegative it is.
Wrong. Formal charge counts lone pairs in full for the atom that holds them. Only the bonding electrons are split.
Wrong. Neutral molecules can have formal charges too, such as O3 and CO. The formal charges just add up to the overall charge.

p: Both are ways of counting electrons on an atom. They use different rules. Formal charge pretends every bond is shared 50/50. Each atom keeps its lone-pair electrons plus half of its bonding electrons.
Oxidation state pretends every bond is fully ionic. The more electronegative atom (the one that pulls electrons harder) gets all the bonding electrons. Same molecule, two different numbers.

mem: Formal charge: bonds shared equally (50/50).
Oxidation state: bonding electrons go to the more electronegative atom.
N in NO3- has formal charge +1 but oxidation state +5.
x5B_021.sc: Ask: 'Do I split the bond or give it away?' Split means formal charge. Give away means oxidation state.
x5B_021.trap: Students swap the two definitions. Remember that formal charge ignores electronegativity completely.
x5B_021.plain: Two kids split a pizza. Formal charge says each gets exactly half. Oxidation state says the hungrier kid takes the whole thing.

ox: Wrong. NO2+ is linear O=N=O with two double bonds, so bond order is 2. Higher bond order means shorter bonds.
Wrong, and this is the tempting choice. Nitrite has resonance, but its bond order is 1.5, which is higher than nitrate's 4/3. So its bonds are shorter.
Correct. Nitrate has one double bond shared across three N-O links, so the average bond order is 4/3. That is the lowest of the four, so the bonds are the longest.
Wrong. NO has a bond order of about 2.5, which is higher than nitrate, so its bond is very short. Do not pick it just because it is a small, odd molecule.

p: Bond order is how many bonds join two atoms on average. A single bond is 1, a double is 2. Higher bond order pulls atoms closer together, so the bond is shorter and stronger.
With resonance, the bond order is an average. Count all the bonds between the two atoms, then divide by the number of equivalent positions.

mem: Higher bond order means shorter, stronger bond.
Resonance averages the bond order over equivalent bonds.

fm.f: Bond order = (total N-O bonds) / (number of N-O links), where total bonds counts a double as 2 and a single as 1
fm.v: Nitrate: one double (2) plus two singles (1 + 1) = 4 bonds over 3 links
fm.why: Resonance spreads the one double bond equally over all three N-O links.
fm.nc: Just add the bonds and divide by 3. No calculator needed.

tb.cap: Average N-O bond order (lower order = longer bond)

x5B_026.trap: Seeing resonance in both nitrite and nitrate and picking nitrite. Always compare the actual averaged bond orders.
x5B_026.plain: Think of holding hands with a friend. Two hands gripped tight keep you close. One hand shared among three friends leaves everyone farther apart.

ox: Correct. The nitrogen lone pair spreads into the C=O pi system. This gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, so it is shorter and rotation is restricted. The group is flat.
Wrong. Amide nitrogen is effectively sp2, not sp3. An sp3 nitrogen would rotate freely. Calling it sp3 is the trap.
Wrong. Tertiary amides have no N-H and are still rigid. So hydrogen bonding cannot be the cause.
Wrong. Sterics (crowding) cannot make a bond shorter. Only extra bonding character shortens a bond.

p: Resonance means electrons are spread over several atoms. In an amide, the lone pair on nitrogen can slide toward the carbon and push the C=O pi electrons onto oxygen. One drawing then shows C=N and a negative O.
The real molecule is a blend of both drawings. So the C-N bond is part single, part double. Double bonds are shorter and cannot twist easily.

mem: Amide C-N has partial double-bond character.
Amide N is planar and sp2-like.
Restricted rotation is why peptide bonds are rigid.
x5B_029.trap: Choosing hybridization or hydrogen bonding. The key idea is resonance delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair.
x5B_029.plain: A rope tied loosely between two posts spins freely. Tie it twice and it is stiff. Resonance gives the C-N bond that extra tie.

ox: Wrong. Putting charge on the less electronegative carbon helps a little. But this carbon has only six electrons, and a missing octet matters more.
Wrong. The charge is the same overall, but the structures are not equally stable. Resonance contributors are ranked by octets and charge placement.
Correct. In (CH3)2C=OH+ every atom has a full octet. Full octets beat charge placement, so this is the major contributor.
Wrong. Moving the pi pair from C=O onto oxygen gives a valid second structure. So resonance exists here.

p: Resonance contributors are different drawings of the same molecule. Some drawings are better than others. The best drawing is the one that looks most like the real molecule.
Rank them in this order. First, full octets (eight electrons around each atom). Then fewer charges. Then negative charge on the more electronegative atom, positive on the less. Octets come first.

mem: Rule 1: complete octets win.
Rule 2: fewer formal charges.
Rule 3: negative on electronegative atom, positive on less electronegative.
A carbocation has only six electrons, so it is a poor contributor.
x5B_030.trap: Picking the carbocation because carbon is less electronegative. Octet beats electronegativity.
x5B_030.plain: When picking a team photo, you choose the one where nobody is missing. A photo with a missing person is a worse picture even if it has a nicer background.

ox: Wrong. The hydrogens do repel each other slightly, but that would widen the angle, not narrow it. This is not the main cause.
Correct. Lone pairs take up more room near oxygen and repel harder than bonding pairs. They push the two O-H bonds closer, giving 104.5 degrees.
Wrong. Water's oxygen has four electron domains, so it is treated as sp3. Calling it sp2 is a trap.
Wrong. The angle is the same for single gas-phase molecules with no neighbors. So hydrogen bonding between molecules does not cause it.

p: VSEPR says electron groups around an atom push apart as far as they can. Water's oxygen has four groups: two bonds and two lone pairs. Four groups would ideally sit at 109.5 degrees.
A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so it spreads out and takes more space. It shoves the bonds together, shrinking the angle to about 104.5 degrees.

mem: Lone pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair repulsion.
Water: 2 bonds, 2 lone pairs, about 104.5 degrees.
Ideal tetrahedral angle is 109.5 degrees.
x5B_032.trap: Blaming hydrogen bonding. That is between molecules, but bond angle is inside one molecule.
x5B_032.plain: Two fat kids and two thin kids on a seat. The fat kids take more room, so the thin kids get squeezed closer.

ox: Wrong. Bent shapes come from molecules with three or four electron domains plus lone pairs. Xe here has five domains, and the three lone pairs are positioned to leave a straight line.
Correct. Xe has five domains: two bonds and three lone pairs. The lone pairs sit in the equatorial spots, so the two F atoms are axial, 180 degrees apart, which is linear.
Wrong. Trigonal planar needs three bonded atoms and no lone pairs. XeF2 has only two bonded atoms.
Wrong. T-shaped needs three bonded atoms and two lone pairs. XeF2 has only two bonded atoms.

p: When a central atom has five electron domains (bonds or lone pairs), they form a trigonal bipyramid. Three positions are equatorial (around the middle) and two are axial (top and bottom).

Lone pairs prefer equatorial spots because there they have fewer close neighbors. In XeF2, three lone pairs fill all equatorial spots. The two F atoms are left on top and bottom, giving a straight line.

mem: 5 domains, trigonal bipyramidal: 1 lone pair = seesaw (SF4), 2 lone pairs = T-shaped (ClF3), 3 lone pairs = linear (XeF2).
Lone pairs go equatorial.
Lone pairs do not always mean bent.
x5B_036.trap: Assuming any molecule with lone pairs is bent. Count domains first and place lone pairs equatorial.
x5B_036.plain: Picture a spinning top. Three heavy kids sit around the middle ring and two light ones sit at the top and bottom, in a perfect line.

ox: Wrong. This is reversed. Water has two lone pairs, which squeeze the angle most, so it has the smallest angle.
Correct. CH4 has no lone pairs (109.5 degrees), NH3 has one (about 107), and H2O has two (about 104.5). More lone pairs means a smaller angle.
Wrong. Methane has no lone pairs, so it has the largest angle, not NH3.
Wrong. Only CH4 has the ideal 109.5 degrees. Lone pairs compress the angles in NH3 and H2O.

p: CH4, NH3 and H2O each have four electron domains. So each starts from the tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonded pairs. Each lone pair squeezes the bonds closer together. Methane has 0 lone pairs, ammonia 1, water 2. The angle shrinks step by step.

mem: CH4 = 109.5 degrees (0 lone pairs).
NH3 = about 107 degrees (1 lone pair).
H2O = about 104.5 degrees (2 lone pairs).
x5B_042.sc: Rank by lone pairs. More lone pairs equals smaller angle.
x5B_042.trap: Thinking the same electron geometry means the same bond angle.
x5B_042.plain: Squeeze a balloon animal's legs together. The more fat bubbles you add on the other side, the tighter the legs get pushed.

ox: Wrong. Distance to the nucleus differs only slightly. The real reason is how many 90 degree neighbors each site has.
Wrong. Electronegative atoms do favor axial sites, but no rule reserves them. The lone pair goes equatorial because of repulsion counts, not a reservation.
Wrong. SF4 geometry is a VSEPR effect. Pi systems are not involved.
Correct. An equatorial site has only two neighbors at 90 degrees. An axial site has three. The bulky lone pair goes where fewer 90 degree repulsions occur.

concept.t: Lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramid
p: In a trigonal bipyramid, neighbors at 90 degrees repel much more than neighbors at 120 degrees. An axial position has three neighbors at 90 degrees. An equatorial position has only two.
A lone pair is bulky and repels strongly. So it takes the equatorial spot to feel less repulsion. That is why SF4 is seesaw, ClF3 is T-shaped, and XeF2 is linear.

mem: Lone pairs prefer equatorial positions.
90 degree repulsion is stronger than 120 degree.
SF4 = seesaw, ClF3 = T-shaped, XeF2 = linear.
x5B_044.trap: Choosing electronegativity or distance. The deciding factor is the count of 90 degree neighbors.
x5B_044.plain: At a crowded table, the biggest kid sits at the end seat where only two others are close, not the middle where three are.

ox: Wrong. Atoms in an aromatic ring are sp2, so the ring can be flat with overlapping p orbitals. sp3 is the trap.
Correct. Pyridine's N is sp2. Its p orbital gives one electron to the aromatic pi system. Its lone pair sits in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, which is free to grab a proton.
Wrong. That describes pyrrole, where the N lone pair is part of the pi system. In pyridine the N already gives one p electron.
Wrong. N has three domains (two ring bonds and one lone pair), so it is sp2, not sp.

p: Aromatic rings are flat and have six pi electrons in p orbitals. Pyridine's nitrogen has three domains, so it is sp2. Its p orbital holds one electron that joins the ring's pi system.
The lone pair is in an sp2 orbital pointing outward in the plane. It is not needed for aromaticity, so it is available to take a proton. That makes pyridine a base.

mem: Pyridine N: sp2, lone pair in plane, basic.
Pyrrole N: lone pair in the pi system, not basic.
Aromatic = flat, 6 pi electrons.
x5B_050.trap: Mixing up pyridine and pyrrole. Check where the lone pair is.
x5B_050.plain: The ring is a circle of kids holding hands. The nitrogen kid holds hands with one arm only and keeps a spare hand free to wave outward.

ox: Wrong. The central carbon has two sigma bonds, so it is sp, not sp2. Coplanar is also wrong.
Wrong. The central carbon is sp, but the two pi bonds use perpendicular p orbitals, so the ends are twisted 90 degrees, not coplanar.
Wrong. sp2 would need three sigma bonds. The central carbon has only two.
Correct. The central carbon has two sigma bonds, so it is sp and linear. Its two p orbitals are perpendicular, so the two CH2 planes are twisted 90 degrees.

p: Count sigma bonds and lone pairs to find hybridization. The central carbon of allene has two sigma bonds, so it is sp. It has two leftover p orbitals at right angles to each other.
Each p orbital makes one pi bond with a neighboring carbon. A CH2 plane must be perpendicular to its own pi bond. So the two CH2 groups are turned 90 degrees from each other.

mem: 2 domains = sp, 3 = sp2, 4 = sp3.
Two pi bonds on one carbon use perpendicular p orbitals.
Allene ends are perpendicular.
x5B_053.trap: Assuming all alkene carbons are sp2 and flat. A carbon with two double bonds is sp.
x5B_053.plain: Hold two pencils in a line. Now twist one end so it points a different way. The two ends are not flat on the same table.

ox: Correct. 6 C-C sigma + 6 C-H sigma = 12 sigma. Six pi electrons make three pi bonds, delocalized around the ring.
Wrong. This misses three sigma bonds. Each of the six C-C links has a sigma bond, plus six C-H bonds, so 12.
Wrong. This ignores the C-H sigma bonds and counts six pi bonds from six pi electrons. Each pi bond holds two electrons.
Wrong. The sigma count of 12 is right, but there are only three pi bonds, not six.

concept.t: Sigma and pi bonds in benzene
p: Every single bond is one sigma bond. A double bond is one sigma plus one pi. Sigma bonds are formed by head-on overlap. Pi bonds form from side-by-side overlap of p orbitals.
Benzene has six carbon-carbon links and six carbon-hydrogen bonds, giving 12 sigma bonds. Its six pi electrons make three pi bonds, spread over the whole ring.

mem: Single bond = 1 sigma. Double = 1 sigma + 1 pi.
Each pi bond holds 2 electrons.
Benzene: 12 sigma, 3 pi.

fm.f: Total sigma = (C-C links) + (C-H bonds); pi bonds = pi electrons / 2
fm.v: C-C links = 6, C-H bonds = 6, pi electrons = 6
fm.why: Every connection has exactly one sigma bond, and each pi bond uses two electrons.

x5B_061.trap: Confusing six pi electrons with six pi bonds. Divide by 2.
x5B_061.plain: Sigma bonds are the frame of a tent. Pi bonds are the cloth cover draped around the top. Every connection has a pole, but only some have cloth.

ox: Correct. In NH3 the N-H dipoles point toward N, the same way as the lone pair, so they add. In NF3 the N-F dipoles point toward F, opposite the lone pair, so they nearly cancel.
Wrong. NF3 is trigonal pyramidal like NH3, not planar. The lone pair on N keeps it pyramidal.
Wrong. Fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen. That is why the dipoles point toward F.
Wrong. Nitrogen in NF3 still has one lone pair. Without it, the molecule would be planar.

concept.t: Dipole moment as a vector sum
p: A dipole is a separation of charge. Each polar bond has an arrow pointing toward the more electronegative atom. A lone pair also adds a dipole pointing away from the nucleus.
The molecule's overall dipole is the sum of all arrows. In NH3 the arrows point the same way and add up. In NF3 the bond arrows point the opposite way from the lone pair, so they mostly cancel.

mem: Dipole = vector sum of bond dipoles and lone pair.
Dipoles point toward the more electronegative atom.
NH3 about 1.5 D; NF3 about 0.2 D.
x5B_069.trap: Assuming more polar bonds always means a larger dipole. Direction matters.
x5B_069.plain: Tug of war. In NH3 everyone pulls the same direction, so the rope moves a lot. In NF3 the teams pull against each other and it barely moves.

ox: Wrong. Hexane is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with no net dipole, so it has almost no response to the rod.
Wrong. CS2 is linear S=C=S, so its bond dipoles cancel. It has no net dipole.
Correct. CH2Cl2 is tetrahedral with two Cl and two H, so the bond dipoles do not cancel. It has a net dipole, so the molecules orient and are pulled toward the rod.
Wrong. Benzene is flat and symmetric, so the dipoles cancel. It has no net dipole.

p: A polar molecule has a net dipole: one end is slightly positive and the other slightly negative. In an electric field, these molecules rotate and line up, then get pulled toward a charged rod.
Whether a molecule is polar depends on shape. If polar bonds are arranged symmetrically, they cancel. If not, they add up. CH2Cl2 is not symmetric, so it is polar.

mem: Symmetric molecules (CO2, CS2, benzene, CCl4) are nonpolar.
Polar molecules are attracted to charged objects.
Polarity depends on both bond polarity and shape.
x5B_073.trap: Choosing a molecule with polar bonds but symmetric shape, such as CS2 with its cancelling dipoles.
x5B_073.plain: A magnet pulls on a bar with a north and a south end. A perfectly round ball has no ends to grab, so it hardly reacts.

ox: Wrong. Ion-dipole forces involve full charges, so they are stronger than hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bond is second.
Correct. Ion-dipole is strongest because full charges are involved. Then hydrogen bonds, then ordinary dipole-dipole, then London dispersion for similar-sized molecules.
Wrong. Dipole-dipole is weaker than both hydrogen bonding and ion-dipole. H-bonds are a special strong type of dipole-dipole.
Wrong. This reverses the order. For similar-sized molecules, London dispersion is the weakest.

p: Forces between particles get stronger when the charges involved get bigger. Ion-dipole involves a full ion charge and a partial charge. It is the strongest.

Hydrogen bonds are strong because H bonded to N, O or F is very exposed and positive. Ordinary dipole-dipole forces come next. London dispersion is weakest for small molecules, though it grows with size.

mem: Ion-dipole > H-bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion.
H bonds need H on N, O or F.
Large molecules can have large dispersion forces.
x5B_080.mn: I Have Dull Legs: Ion-dipole, Hydrogen bond, Dipole-dipole, London dispersion (strongest to weakest).
x5B_080.trap: Putting hydrogen bonds at the top. Full charges beat partial charges.
x5B_080.plain: Magnets: a full-strength magnet beats a weak fridge magnet, which beats the slight stickiness of dust.

ox: Wrong. HF forms hydrogen bonds, giving it the highest boiling point of the group, near 20 degrees Celsius.
Correct. HCl has no hydrogen bonding and the fewest electrons among HCl, HBr and HI. So it has the weakest dispersion forces and the lowest boiling point.
Wrong. HBr has more electrons than HCl, so stronger dispersion forces and a higher boiling point.
Wrong. HI has the largest electron cloud of HCl, HBr and HI, so it has the strongest dispersion forces and a higher boiling point than HCl.

concept.t: Boiling point trends in hydrogen halides
p: Boiling point depends on how strongly molecules attract each other. Larger molecules have more electrons, so London dispersion forces (temporary attractions) are stronger.
HF is special: H bonded to F makes strong hydrogen bonds, so it boils much higher than expected. Among HCl, HBr and HI, boiling point rises with size. So HCl is lowest.

mem: Boiling point rises HCl < HBr < HI.
HF is highest because of hydrogen bonding.
More electrons means stronger dispersion.
x5B_081.trap: Assuming the lightest molecule always has the lowest boiling point. HF breaks the trend.
x5B_081.plain: Small Velcro patches barely stick. Big ones stick well. HF has glue on top of Velcro.

ox: Wrong. The two isomers have the same formula and the same molar mass. Mass cannot explain the difference.
Correct. In the ortho isomer the OH and NO2 groups are next to each other and hydrogen bond within one molecule. That leaves fewer H-bonds between molecules, so it boils lower.
Wrong. The para isomer has a large dipole and forms hydrogen bonds with other molecules. It is not nonpolar.
Wrong. The ortho isomer does hydrogen bond. It does so inside the molecule, not between molecules.

p: Boiling needs molecules to break away from each other. Hydrogen bonds between molecules (intermolecular) hold them together, so they raise the boiling point.

In o-nitrophenol the OH and NO2 groups are neighbors, so the H bond forms inside the molecule (intramolecular), making a ring. Little H bonding is left for neighboring molecules, so it boils lower. In the para isomer the groups are too far apart, so H bonds form between molecules.

mem: Intermolecular H-bonds raise boiling point.
Intramolecular H-bonds lower it.
Ortho groups are neighbors; para groups are on opposite sides.
x5B_084.trap: Thinking that any hydrogen bonding raises boiling point. Only bonds between molecules count.
x5B_084.plain: A kid who holds his own hand cannot hold a friend's hand. Fewer links to others means he leaves the group easily.

ox: Wrong. This reverses the trend. Stronger intermolecular forces mean a HIGHER boiling point, so ethanol cannot be lowest.
Wrong. This puts propane above acetaldehyde. Propane has only weak dispersion forces, so it boils lower than the polar acetaldehyde.
Correct. Propane has only dispersion forces (bp about -42 C). Acetaldehyde adds dipole-dipole attraction from its polar C=O (bp about 20 C). Ethanol has an O-H, so it hydrogen bonds (bp 78 C).
Wrong. This puts acetaldehyde above ethanol. Acetaldehyde has oxygen but no O-H, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The trap is thinking any oxygen means H-bonding.

p: Boiling means pulling molecules away from their neighbors. The harder they stick together, the more heat you need. Sticking forces between molecules are called intermolecular forces (IMFs).

From weakest to strongest: dispersion (all molecules), dipole-dipole (polar molecules), hydrogen bonding (H on N, O or F attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F). When molar masses are similar, the strongest extra force decides.

mem: Similar mass: H-bond > dipole-dipole > dispersion only for boiling point.
H-bond donor needs H bonded to N, O or F.
A C=O alone makes dipole-dipole, not H-bond donation.
x5B_090.sc: Look for O-H or N-H in the formula first. If present, that compound boils highest.
x5B_090.trap: Assuming oxygen alone means hydrogen bonding. The hydrogen must be attached to O, N or F.
x5B_090.plain: Think of kids holding hands in a crowd. Propane kids barely touch, acetaldehyde kids link pinkies, and ethanol kids grip hands tightly, so ethanol is hardest to pull apart.

ox: Wrong. Pure p orbitals sit at 90 degrees and could not give four equal bonds at 109.5 degrees. The trap is forgetting that carbon hybridizes before bonding.
Wrong. sp2 carbon has three electron domains (trigonal planar, as in alkenes). Each ethane carbon has four sigma bonds, so it is not sp2.
Correct. Each ethane carbon has four sigma bonds, so it is sp3 and tetrahedral. Each C-H bond is head-on overlap of a carbon sp3 hybrid with a hydrogen 1s orbital.
Wrong. Hydrogen has only one valence orbital, the 1s, so it cannot hybridize. The trap is assuming both atoms must hybridize.

p: Hybridization means mixing atomic orbitals to make new equal orbitals. Carbon mixes one s and three p orbitals into four sp3 orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5 degrees).
A sigma bond is head-on overlap of orbitals along the bond axis. Hydrogen only has a 1s orbital, so it just uses that.

mem: 4 electron domains = sp3, 109.5 degrees.
3 domains = sp2 (120 degrees), 2 domains = sp (180 degrees).
Hydrogen always uses 1s.
x5B_091.mn: Count the domains: 4 = sp3, 3 = sp2, 2 = sp. The exponent plus s gives the domain count (sp3 = 1 s + 3 p = 4).
x5B_091.trap: Choosing a pure p orbital or sp2 because you forget to count all four sigma bonds on carbon.
x5B_091.plain: Carbon takes four different tools and blends them into four identical tools, so all four arms reach out evenly. Hydrogen only owns one tool, so it uses that.

ox: Wrong. Water hydrogen bonds extensively, which keeps molecules in the liquid and lowers vapor pressure.
Correct. Diethyl ether has no O-H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself. Only weak dipole and dispersion forces hold it, so molecules escape easily (bp 35 C).
Wrong. Ethanol has an O-H and hydrogen bonds, so its vapor pressure is lower than ether's. The trap is picking it because it is a familiar volatile liquid.
Wrong. Glycerol has three OH groups and many hydrogen bonds, giving it the lowest vapor pressure of the four.

p: Vapor pressure is the pressure of gas above a liquid when evaporation and condensation balance. It shows how easily molecules escape the liquid.
Weak intermolecular forces mean easy escape and high vapor pressure. Strong forces mean low vapor pressure and a higher boiling point. Vapor pressure and boiling point move in opposite directions.

mem: Weak IMFs = high vapor pressure = low boiling point.
Hydrogen bonding lowers vapor pressure.
More OH groups = stronger H-bonding.
x5B_093.trap: Picking water or ethanol because they are common volatile liquids, ignoring that hydrogen bonding traps molecules.
x5B_093.plain: Sticky candy stays in the bowl, but dry beads roll right out. Ether is the dry beads.

ox: Wrong. Both compounds have the same molar mass (60) and similar electron counts, so dispersion forces are about equal. The trap is using 'more electrons' when there are not more.
Wrong. 1-Propanol has an O-H and does hydrogen bond. The real difference is how strongly each pairs up.
Wrong. Pure acetic acid is barely ionized. It is a weak acid and stays mostly molecular.

Correct. The carboxyl group has an O-H donor and a C=O acceptor, so two molecules form a cyclic dimer joined by two hydrogen bonds. The polar C=O adds extra attraction, so the boiling point is higher.

p: A hydrogen bond forms between an H on O, N or F and a lone pair on another O, N or F. Alcohols make one chain of these bonds per OH.

A carboxylic acid has both a donor (O-H) and an acceptor (C=O) side by side. Two acids can lock together as a ring (dimer) with two hydrogen bonds. This acts like a bigger, heavier molecule that is harder to boil.

mem: Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass.
Dimers form from two H-bonds between two acids.
Pure carboxylic acids are barely ionized.
x5B_095.trap: Choosing a reason based on mass or ionization when the molar masses are equal and the real cause is double hydrogen bonding.
x5B_095.plain: Two people can hold one hand each, or they can hold both hands with each other in a tight circle. The double grip is much harder to break.

ox: Wrong. SiO2 is covalent, not ionic. Both oxides are made from nonmetal-like covalent bonds.
Wrong. Both Si-O and C=O bonds are polar. Bond polarity does not explain the huge melting difference.
Wrong. CO2 is nonpolar overall but still has weak dispersion forces. 'No forces at all' is false.
Correct. SiO2 is a network solid, a giant 3-D lattice of Si-O covalent bonds. Melting it breaks those bonds. CO2 is separate small molecules held by weak dispersion forces.

p: A network solid is one giant molecule where every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbors, like quartz or diamond. To melt it you must break covalent bonds, which takes huge energy.
A molecular solid is made of separate molecules. To melt or sublime it you only overcome weak forces between molecules, so it changes phase at low temperature.

mem: Network solids: diamond, quartz (SiO2), graphite. Very high melting points.
Molecular solids melt by breaking IMFs, not bonds.
Si does not form stable pi bonds with O, so SiO2 builds a network.
x5B_098.trap: Thinking the formulas look alike (XO2), so the structures must be alike.
x5B_098.plain: A network solid is a chain-link fence welded everywhere. CO2 is a pile of loose marbles you can just scoop up.

ox: Correct. Soap is amphipathic. Its nonpolar tails hide in the center away from water, and its charged carboxylate heads face the water on the outside.
Wrong. That is a reverse micelle, which forms in nonpolar solvents. In water the heads, not the tails, must face outward.
Wrong. Bilayers are typical of double-tailed lipids such as phospholipids. A single-tailed soap forms small spheres (micelles).
Wrong. Above the critical micelle concentration soap molecules aggregate. The trap is forgetting that amphipathic molecules self-organize.

p: An amphipathic molecule has a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and a water-fearing (hydrophobic) tail. In water, the tails clump together to avoid water, while the heads stay in contact with it.
This makes a sphere called a micelle. Oily dirt sits in the center, so soap can carry grease away in water.

mem: Micelle in water: tails in, heads out.
Single tail = micelle. Double tail = bilayer.
Nonpolar solvent: reverse micelle.
x5B_099.trap: Flipping which part faces water. Remember: hydrophobic tails hide from water.
x5B_099.plain: Like kids in a snowball fight who huddle in a ball with their cold, wet gloves hidden in the middle and their warm jackets outside.

ox: Wrong. More electrons make a larger ion, which weakens ionic attraction. Electron count matters for dispersion forces, not lattice energy.
Wrong. Polarizability affects dispersion and covalent character. Lattice energy depends on charge and distance.
Correct. F- is much smaller than I-, so Na+ and F- sit closer. Coulomb attraction rises as distance falls, so NaF has the greater lattice energy.
Wrong. Equal charges do not make equal lattice energy. The ion sizes differ, so the distance differs.

p: Lattice energy is the energy released when separate ions come together to form a solid crystal. A bigger number means a more stable, harder-to-melt solid.
It follows Coulomb's law: it grows with larger charges and shrinks with larger distance between ion centers. If charges are equal, the smaller ions win.

mem: Lattice energy rises with charge and falls with ion size.
Charge matters more than size.
Higher lattice energy means higher melting point.

fm.f: Coulomb attraction is proportional to (q1 x q2) / r, where q1 and q2 = ion charges and r = distance between ion centers
fm.v: Both compounds: q1 = +1, q2 = -1. r(NaF) is smaller than r(NaI)
fm.s: Same top number, smaller bottom for NaF, so NaF is larger
fm.why: Same charges mean only distance can differ.
fm.nc: No numbers needed. Just compare which ion is smaller.

x5B_102.trap: Choosing the larger ion because it has more electrons or is more polarizable.
x5B_102.plain: Two magnets stuck together are harder to pull apart than two magnets with a thick book between them. Small ions are the magnets with no book.

ox: Wrong. Ionic crystals are held by ionic attractions, not covalent bonds. Those attractions are strong.
Wrong. Ionic solids have no free-moving electrons. Metals do, and metals bend instead of shatter.
Wrong. Ionic attractions are strong, which is why melting points are high. Brittleness is not from weak attraction.
Correct. A blow shifts one layer so like charges line up (cation by cation, anion by anion). They repel and the crystal splits along that plane.

p: In an ionic crystal, positive and negative ions alternate in a pattern, so every ion has opposite-charge neighbors. This is stable.
If a layer slides by one ion, same charges end up side by side. They repel strongly and the crystal cracks. Metals differ: their shared electron sea lets layers slide without repulsion.

mem: Ionic solids: brittle, high mp, conduct only when molten or dissolved.
Metals: malleable and ductile.
Brittleness comes from like-charge repulsion.
x5B_104.trap: Blaming weak bonding. Ionic bonds are strong; the shape of the repulsion causes the break.
x5B_104.plain: Picture a checkerboard of red and blue magnets. Slide one row over by one square and now reds face reds. They push apart and the board snaps.

ox: Correct. Cs is among the least electronegative elements and F is the most electronegative, so their difference is the largest. That gives the most ionic character.
Wrong. Li is more electronegative than Cs and I is less than F, so the difference is smaller. Small Li+ also polarizes big I-, adding covalent character.
Wrong. Na-Cl is ionic, but Na is more electronegative than Cs and Cl less than F, so the difference is smaller than Cs-F.
Wrong. Be is small and highly polarizing, so Be-Cl is largely covalent.

p: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons. The bigger the difference between two atoms, the more the electrons are pulled to one side. A very big difference means ionic bonding.
Electronegativity rises toward the top right of the periodic table (fluorine is highest) and falls toward the bottom left (cesium is lowest).

mem: Most ionic: far left bottom metal with far right top nonmetal (Cs-F).
Electronegativity: F > O > N,Cl.
Small, highly charged cations make bonds more covalent.
x5B_107.trap: Picking the familiar salt (NaCl) rather than comparing electronegativity differences.
x5B_107.plain: In tug-of-war, a huge strong kid against a tiny kid takes the whole rope. That is Cs and F: F takes the electron completely.

ox: Wrong. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images with the same connectivity. These two have different connectivity, and neither is chiral.
Wrong. Diastereomers are stereoisomers, so they share connectivity. These do not.
Wrong. Conformers interconvert by rotating single bonds. Turning butane into isobutane requires breaking and making bonds.
Correct. Same formula (C4H10) but different atom connections: a straight chain versus a branched chain. These are constitutional isomers.

p: Isomers share a molecular formula. Constitutional (structural) isomers connect their atoms in a different order. Stereoisomers connect atoms the same way but differ in 3-D arrangement.
Stereoisomers include enantiomers (mirror images) and diastereomers (not mirror images). Conformers are the same molecule twisted by bond rotation.

mem: Different connectivity = constitutional isomers.
Same connectivity, different 3-D = stereoisomers.
Conformers need only bond rotation.
x5B_108.sc: Draw both. If you must break a bond to convert them, they are constitutional isomers.
x5B_108.trap: Confusing 'different shape' with stereoisomers. Branching changes the connectivity.
x5B_108.plain: Same Lego bricks built into two different models. They use identical pieces but the pieces are joined differently.

ox: Wrong. Enantiomers have identical boiling points, so distillation cannot separate them.
Wrong. Enantiomers dissolve identically in achiral solvents such as water.
Correct. Reacting with one pure chiral enantiomer makes diastereomeric salts. Diastereomers have different solubilities, so they can be separated by crystallization and then converted back.
Wrong. Silica is achiral, so it interacts with both enantiomers equally. You would need a chiral stationary phase.

p: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of two enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral setting, so ordinary methods cannot split them.

Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, and they DO have different physical properties. Reacting the mixture with one pure chiral reagent turns enantiomers into diastereomers, which can be separated.

mem: Enantiomers: same mp, bp, solubility (achiral conditions).
Diastereomers: different physical properties.
Resolve with a chiral resolving agent, then recover each enantiomer.
x5B_112.trap: Choosing a standard separation method that only works on differences enantiomers do not have.
x5B_112.plain: Your left and right shoes look identical to a plain box. But hand each a left glove and the pairs now differ, so you can tell them apart.

ox: Wrong. 30% is the enantiomeric excess (ee), the extra amount of (+) beyond a 50:50 mix. It is not the percent of (+).
Correct. ee = 6/20 = 30%. The other 70% is racemic and splits 35% and 35%. So (+) = 30% + 35% = 65%.
Wrong. 70% is the racemic portion of the sample, not the (+) enantiomer's share.
Wrong. 35% is the percent of the (-) enantiomer. The question asks for (+).

p: Optical rotation is how much a sample twists plane-polarized light. A racemic mix twists 0 because the two enantiomers cancel. Enantiomeric excess (ee) is the extra of one enantiomer: ee = observed rotation / pure rotation.
The ee part is all one enantiomer. The rest is a 50:50 mix. Add half of the rest to the ee to get the major enantiomer percent.

mem: ee = observed / pure x 100%.
Major % = ee + (100 - ee)/2. Minor % = (100 - ee)/2.
Racemic mixture has rotation 0.

fm.f: ee = observed rotation / pure rotation, where ee = enantiomeric excess; then (+) % = ee + (100% - ee)/2
fm.why: The excess is all (+), and the rest is split evenly.

x5B_116.trap: Stopping at 30% (the ee) instead of adding the half of the racemic portion.
x5B_116.plain: A tug-of-war where 35 kids pull each side cancel out, and 30 extra kids join only the left team. The left team has 65.
